transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Lee. Thank you. Um… I think what finally pushed me to come in is that I’m noticing it more at work. I manage health services, and I’ll sit down to do something like an EPIC quality report, or I’ll be in a clinic metrics meeting really intending to follow along, and then a few minutes later I realize my mind has wandered completely. I’m rereading the same numbers or I’ve missed the main point of what was just discussed.

It’s embarrassing to say, because I do try hard to stay on top of things, and I don’t want it to sound like I’m not paying attention on purpose. It’s just been happening enough that I thought maybe I should ask someone about it.
Can you tell me approximately when you first started noticing these attention and concentration difficulties—has this been a lifelong pattern, or did it start more recently?

I wouldn’t say I noticed it my whole life, at least not in a way that felt like a real problem. It’s been more since my promotion… about two years and four months ago, I think.

When my portfolio got bigger, the systems I used to rely on just started not being enough, and that’s when I began realizing I was having trouble keeping up with the attention and concentration piece. I don’t know if that answers it the way you mean.
Have you noticed loud snoring, gasping, or choking during sleep, or has anyone told you that you stop breathing while you sleep?

Um… not that I’m aware of. No one has told me I stop breathing or anything like that. I don’t think I gasp or choke in my sleep, at least I haven’t noticed it. I’m not sure how much I’d know myself, but as far as I know, no.
Over the past several months, have you found yourself worrying excessively about a number of different things—like work, health, or family—and having a hard time controlling that worry?

I don’t think so… not excessively, anyway. I mean, I worry about work sometimes, like anyone would, but I wouldn’t say it’s constant or that I can’t control it. At least, I don’t think that’s the main issue. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Over the past couple of months, have you noticed a persistent low mood or a loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy?

I don’t think so, no. I mean, I have off days, or I get frustrated, but I wouldn’t describe it as a persistent low mood. And I still enjoy things when I actually make time for them. I don’t think that’s really been the issue… if that makes sense.
Do you often feel excessively sleepy or fatigued during the day, even after what you think was a full night's sleep?

I don’t think so, not excessively. I mean, I get tired sometimes during the day, but I wouldn’t say I’m falling asleep or anything like that after a full night’s sleep. It feels more like normal tired, if that makes sense.
Have you noticed any recent weight gain, feeling unusually cold, dry skin, or constipation over the past several months?

Not really, no. I haven’t noticed anything like that in a clear way. My weight seems about the same, and I don’t think I’ve been unusually cold or anything. I mean, dry skin happens here and there, but nothing that seemed out of the ordinary. Does that answer what you’re looking for?

Thinking back to when you were in school—say, middle or high school—did you ever have trouble paying attention, staying organized, or finishing tasks, even if it didn't feel like a big problem at the time?

Yes, I think so… although I didn’t really think of it as a “problem” back then. Even in elementary school, teachers would write things like I was bright but careless. My mom used to have to sit with me while I finished homework because I’d lose track of assignments, or I’d forget the book I needed at school.

I always kind of explained it away as being busy or just not trying hard enough, I guess. But looking back, yes, that was probably there earlier than I realized.
Do you often feel restless, fidgety, or have trouble sitting still, or find yourself acting impulsively—like interrupting others or making quick decisions without thinking them through?

I’m not sure I’d describe myself that way, no. I mean, I’ll shift around in a chair sometimes or get a little impatient, but I don’t think I’m especially restless or impulsive. I try not to interrupt people—at least, I hope I don’t. Quick decisions… maybe occasionally, like anyone, but nothing that stands out to me as a major issue. Is that the kind of thing you mean?
Outside of work, do you notice similar problems with attention, organization, or forgetfulness—like at home, managing personal tasks, or in your relationships?

Yes… I mean, I do notice it outside of work too, though I try to keep it from affecting other people. At work it’s probably more obvious—my delays have started affecting clinic reporting deadlines, and sometimes other teams are waiting on me, which I feel really bad about.

And outside of that, I’ve had to step back from leading parts of the volunteer health workshops because I just couldn’t reliably keep all the planning pieces moving. I don’t know if that’s the kind of example you mean, but it’s been frustrating because I do care and I want to be dependable.

Going back to those school years, did those attention and organization struggles actually cause noticeable problems—like grades slipping, trouble with friends, or conflicts at home—before you turned 12?

Before 12… yes, I think there were signs, though I don’t know if I’d say it was dramatic. I remember teachers writing things like I was bright but careless, which was embarrassing, because I was trying. And my mom often had to sit with me to get homework finished because I’d lose track of what I was supposed to do or realize I’d left the book I needed at school.

So… I guess it did cause problems at home, at least with homework. I’m not sure if that’s the kind of “noticeable” you mean.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient demonstrates a longstanding pattern of inattentive symptoms (careless errors, losing track of tasks, forgetfulness, disorganization) that began before age 12, as evidenced by childhood reports of being 'bright but careless' and needing parental assistance with homework. These symptoms have persisted into adulthood and significantly impair functioning across multiple settings (work performance/deadlines, volunteer leadership roles), meeting cross-situational impairment criteria. Hyperactive-impulsive symptoms are notably absent or minimal. Differential diagnoses including generalized anxiety disorder, major depressive disorder, hypothyroidism, and obstructive sleep apnea were systematically ruled out through direct questioning, as the patient denied excessive worry, persistent low mood/anhedonia, cold intolerance/weight changes, and sleep-disordered breathing symptoms. The clinical picture is most consistent with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, predominantly inattentive presentation.
